title: Session 2: Introduction to PsychoPy
text:
Welcome to the second session of our Python and PsychoPy workshop! Let’s take stock of what you can already do. In Session 1, you went from print("Hello world!") to writing your own loops. Along the way, you learned how to:
This is genuinely all the Python you need to run a sophisticated experiment. Today you’ll see why: a real experiment is a list of stimuli, a loop over trials, an if/else for feedback, and an f-string on the screen.
By the end of today, you will have built a working experiment that shows images in random order, collects keyboard responses, and gives feedback on every trial.
Today, we change environment: from UCloud to the PsychoPy Coder on your own laptop. This “Coder” is a simpler editor bundled with PsychoPy, and the Python inside it is the same Python you already know.

title: Session 2: Introduction to PsychoPy
text:
Learning outcomes
After this session, you can:

Open and close a PsychoPy window and explain the draw-flip cycle (prepare, draw, flip) that gives experiments their precise timing.
Present text and image stimuli (TextStim, ImageStim), for a fixed duration (core.wait()) or until a keypress (event.waitKeys()).
Write your own functions with def and parameters, and use them to remove repetition from an experiment script.
Load stimulus files automatically with glob.glob() instead of typing filenames by hand.
Randomise trial order with random.shuffle() and explain why randomisation matters.
Collect and restrict keyboard responses (keyList=['left', 'right']), evaluate them against a rule read from the filename, and give conditional feedback.
Measure reaction times with core.Clock(): reset at stimulus onset, read at the response.

title: 9 · Timing: Measuring How Long Thinking Takes
text:
Thinking takes time
Your experiment runs, and it already produces one measurement: whether each answer was correct. Block 3 adds the second, and for cognitive science the more interesting one: how long the answer took. The idea is old and beautiful: mental work takes time, and the time can be measured. Your own experiment contains a built-in comparison. On a burrow trial, you press the arrow on the burrow’s side: your response goes toward the thing you saw, which is what your attention wants anyway. On a lion trial, you press the opposite arrow: your response goes away from the thing you saw, and to produce it you must override the pull toward the lion first. That overriding is extra mental work, so lion trials should take longer, by tens of milliseconds. Reaction time is how we watch that work happen without opening the head. The same measurement carries your Portfolio 2 experiment: how long a reader lingers on a word tells us how hard that word is to process.
crumbs: 9 · Timing: Measuring How Long Thinking Takes

title: 9 · Timing: Measuring How Long Thinking Takes
text:
A stopwatch object
The tool is core.Clock(): a stopwatch. Create it once, in the setup; reset it to zero at the moment you want to measure from; read it when the thing you are timing has happened.
stopwatch = core.Clock()     # create, once, in the setup
stopwatch.reset()            # zero it: timing starts NOW
rt = stopwatch.getTime()     # read it: seconds since the reset
A small demonstration you can run in a script, no window needed:
from psychopy import core

stopwatch = core.Clock()
stopwatch.reset()
core.wait(1.5)
print(stopwatch.getTime())

Approximately what number is printed?

The clock was zeroed, then the script waited. How much time passed between the reset and the read?


Approximately 1.5, in practice something like 1.5001923: one and a half seconds passed between the reset and the read, plus a sliver of processing time. The clock does not stop at getTime(); it keeps running, and you can read it as often as you like. Reset defines the zero; every read reports the seconds since.
crumbs: 9 · Timing: Measuring How Long Thinking Takes

title: 9 · Timing: Measuring How Long Thinking Takes
text:
Where the reset goes
In a trial, what we want to measure is the gap between stimulus onset and response. Both endpoints matter.
The response end is easy: event.waitKeys() returns at the keypress, so reading the clock on the next line captures it. The onset end is the subtle one, and Chapter 3 prepared you for it: a stimulus appears at one precise moment, the flip. Preparing and drawing take time, so the reset must come after the flip, not before the drawing. In our script, show_stim() ends with the flip, so the reset follows the call directly:
show_stim(image)                                  # ends with win.flip(): onset
stopwatch.reset()                                 # zero AT onset

keys = event.waitKeys(keyList=['left', 'right'])  # returns at the keypress
rt = stopwatch.getTime()                          # seconds from onset to response






🤔 Think first



A student puts stopwatch.reset() before the show_stim(image) call instead of after it. The script runs fine and produces reaction times. What is wrong with them?






Check your thinking





Every reaction time is slightly too long. The clock starts before the stimulus exists: preparing the image and flipping it to the screen take time, and that preparation time is silently added to every trial’s measurement. The participant has not even seen the stimulus while the clock is already running. Reset after the flip, so that zero means “the moment the scene appeared”.











Good to know: how precise is this?





Honest measurement means knowing your instrument. Two small imprecisions are built in: the stimulus appears at a screen refresh, so onset is quantised to the frame (about 17 ms at 60 Hz), and ordinary keyboards add a few milliseconds of their own. Neither can be removed with ordinary hardware, and neither matters for us: both affect all trials equally, and the comparisons we care about, such as lion trials against burrow trials, are differences of tens of milliseconds averaged over trials. Know the noise, design comparisons larger than it.









Summary



core.Clock() is a stopwatch: create once, reset() to define zero, getTime() to read seconds since. For a reaction time, zero must mean stimulus onset, so the reset goes immediately after the flip, and the read goes immediately after waitKeys() returns. The measurement carries about a frame of onset noise and a few milliseconds of keyboard noise, which comparisons across many trials absorb.

title: 9 · Timing: Measuring How Long Thinking Takes
text:
Three clock puzzles, together
Before the clock enters the experiment, three small puzzles about how it behaves. Predict each one before anything is run.

Puzzle 1: the clock keeps running
from psychopy import core

stopwatch = core.Clock()
stopwatch.reset()

core.wait(1)
print(stopwatch.getTime())

core.wait(1)
print(stopwatch.getTime())

Two numbers are printed. Approximately which two? Answer on one line, separated by a space.

Does getTime() stop the clock, or only look at it?


Approximately 1, then 2. Reading the clock does not stop it or reset it; it only looks. The clock runs continuously from the reset, and every read reports the total seconds since that one zero. One reset can serve many reads.




Puzzle 2: reset moves the zero
from psychopy import core

stopwatch = core.Clock()
stopwatch.reset()

core.wait(1)
stopwatch.reset()

core.wait(1)
print(stopwatch.getTime())

One number is printed. Approximately what?

There are two resets. Which one defines the zero that the read is measured from?


Approximately 1, not 2. A reset throws away everything before it and starts the count again: the second reset moved the zero, so the read reports only the second second. This is precisely why one reset per trial works in an experiment: each trial’s reset wipes the previous trial’s time and starts fresh.




Puzzle 3: the misplaced reset, with numbers
Suppose preparing and flipping a large image takes half a second, and the participant responds one second after the stimulus appears. A student writes the reset in the wrong place:
stopwatch.reset()          # reset HERE...
stim.draw()                # takes ~0.5 s in this thought experiment
win.flip()                 # ...stimulus appears now
keys = event.waitKeys()    # participant responds 1 s after onset
rt = stopwatch.getTime()

What reaction time does the script report, in seconds?

The clock started before the drawing. How much time passed between the reset and the keypress, in total?


1.5 seconds, for a response that actually took 1.0. The half second of preparation is silently added, because the zero was set before the stimulus existed. The participant looks half a second slower than they are, on every trial. Zero must mean onset, so the reset goes after the flip.




Puzzle 4: one clock, many trials
The experiment measures twelve trials, but it needs only one clock. Create it once in the setup; inside the loop, reset at each trial’s onset and read at each trial’s response. The reset wipes the previous trial’s time (Puzzle 2), so the same stopwatch serves every trial in turn. A miniature version, with waits standing in for participants:
from psychopy import core

stopwatch = core.Clock()            # once, in the setup

for trial in [1, 2, 3]:
    stopwatch.reset()               # zero at this trial's onset
    core.wait(trial)                # this "participant" takes 1, then 2, then 3 s
    print(stopwatch.getTime())

Three numbers are printed. Approximately which three, in order? One line, separated by spaces.

Does time pile up across trials, or does something wipe it between them?


Approximately 1, 2, 3: each trial’s reset wipes the clock, so each read reports only its own trial’s time. Without the reset inside the loop, the times would pile up, 1, 3, 6, each trial inheriting all the seconds before it. One clock in the setup, one reset per trial at onset, one read per trial at the response: that is the whole pattern, and it is exactly what you will add to the rabbit in Exercise 6.


Stopwatch demo printing sensible numbers? Next: Exercise 6, timing the rabbit.

title: 7 · Responses and Feedback
text:
Block 2 · Learning goals: Collect arrow-key responses, decide from the filename whether they were correct, and show feedback.
So far, our experiment can show stimuli, but it cannot yet interact with our participant. Any key advances the script, and the script never learns which key it was. This chapter changes that in three steps. First we find out what a keypress looks like to Python. Then we restrict which keys count and read out the one that was pressed. Finally we judge the response and answer it with feedback. At the end of the page, these steps click together into one complete trial of the Fleeing Rabbit.

title: 7 · Responses and Feedback
section: Step one: see what a keypress looks like
text:
Step one: see what a keypress looks like
Start with a small discovery. Type this complete script into a file and run it:
from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1280, 720), fullscr=False,
                    color='black', checkTiming=False)
win.flip()

print(event.waitKeys())

win.close()
core.quit()
A black window opens and the script waits. Click on the PsychoPy window first, so your keypress goes to it rather than to the Coder, and then press the spacebar. The window closes, and one thing has been printed to the console.

What exactly is printed to the console?

Close, but PsychoPy has its own, shorter name for that key. And look at the shape of what comes back: it arrives wrapped in something.


['space']. A list, holding one lowercase string. It is a list even for a single keypress, because the function can catch several keys at once. Two useful things follow. To get the key, you index with [0], exactly as in Session 1. And the print-and-press trick works for any key: run the line and press whatever you are curious about, and PsychoPy tells you its name.

title: 7 · Responses and Feedback
text:
Step two: restrict and read
For a real trial, we want two things at once. Only the arrow keys should count, so a stray elbow on the spacebar cannot skip a trial. And we want the pressed key stored in a variable, ready to use. Both come from the same two lines:
1keys = event.waitKeys(keyList=['left', 'right'])
2key = keys[0]

1

keyList names the keys that count. Every other key is simply ignored.

2

The result is a list, as you just discovered. Element [0] is the pressed key: a plain string such as 'left'.


One warning before moving on. If you skip the [0] and compare the list itself, nothing crashes, but every comparison fails: ['left'] == 'left' is False, because a list is never equal to a string. An experiment with this bug marks every answer wrong and never raises an error.

title: 7 · Responses and Feedback
text:
Step three: was it correct?
The script now knows what the participant pressed. To judge the press, it also needs to know what the participant should have pressed. Where does that knowledge live?
In the filenames. Recall the design from the glob chapter: every scene’s name ends in _L or _R, and the suffix records the correct response. A lion on the left means flee right, so that scene is stimulus1_R.jpg. A burrow on the left means dive in left: stimulus3_L.jpg. The tricky lion rule was settled once, when the stimuli were made. The script never reasons about lions; it just reads the suffix, with .endswith() from the warm-up:
if image.endswith('_L.jpg'):
    correct_key = 'left'
else:
    correct_key = 'right'
Every trial now has two facts, held in two variables: correct_key, what should happen, taken from the stimulus; and key, what did happen, taken from the keyboard.

A trial shows stimuli/stimulus8_R.jpg, a burrow on the right. The participant, startled, presses left. What is correct_key on this trial?

correct_key comes from the filename, not from what the participant did. What does the suffix say?


right. The filename ends _R.jpg, so correct_key is 'right', regardless of any keypress. The participant’s left sits in the other variable, key, and the two will disagree. Keeping should and did in separate variables is what makes the next step a one-line comparison.

title: 7 · Responses and Feedback
text:
Step four: feedback
The judgement is now a single comparison, and its outcome picks an image: the escaping rabbit or the triumphant lion, shown for exactly two seconds.
if key == correct_key:
    feedback = visual.ImageStim(win, image='stimuli/success.jpg')
else:
    feedback = visual.ImageStim(win, image='stimuli/failure.jpg')

feedback.draw()
win.flip()
core.wait(2)
Note that the logic arrived as two small decisions rather than one big one: first derive correct_key from the stimulus, then compare it with key. Each piece can be checked on its own, which is what makes small decisions easier to debug than large ones.






🤔 Think first




Why core.wait(2) for the feedback screen rather than event.waitKeys()? (b) The stimulus was already flipped onto the screen. Why does the feedback need its own draw() and flip()?







Check your thinking






Feedback should be brief and identical for everyone, not something to sit on or skip. The computer decides. (b) A flip reveals one prepared scene. Showing something new means preparing again: draw backstage, raise the curtain again. Every screen gets its own draw and flip.

title: 7 · Responses and Feedback
text:
One complete trial
Click the four steps together and you have a full trial: show a scene, collect the response, judge it, answer it. The full experiment is nothing more than this trial, shuffled and looped, and building that is the next page.






🔒 Example code will be available here after the workshop












Tip: a polite emergency exit



Add 'escape' to your keyList and handle it: if key == 'escape': win.close(); core.quit(). Essential once you go fullscreen. It returns as an Advanced task in Exercise 5.








Summary



event.waitKeys(keyList=[...]) restricts which keys count and returns a list; keys[0] is the pressed key as a plain string. Correctness lives in the filenames: the suffix encodes the correct response, lion rule included, and .endswith() reads it into correct_key. One trial holds two facts, what should happen and what did, and feedback is the comparison between them, drawn and flipped like any other screen, for a fixed two seconds.


One trial working? Next: the main exercise of the day.

title: 5 · Functions: Write Once, Use Many Times
text:
The repetition problem
Consider what showing anything on screen has required so far: prepare, draw, flip, wait, four lines, every single time. Two text screens and an image is twelve lines. And suppose we want something slightly more ambitious: a rabbit that visits all four corners of the window, half a second in each. A stimulus object’s position can be changed after it is created (pic.pos = (0.5, 0.5)), so we prepare the ImageStim once and then move, draw, flip, and wait for every corner. Written out in full, that looks like this:
from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1280, 720), fullscr=False,
                    color='black', checkTiming=False)

pic = visual.ImageStim(win, image='rabbit.jpg', size=0.5)

pic.pos = (-0.5, 0.5)    # top left
pic.draw()
win.flip()
core.wait(0.5)

pic.pos = (0.5, 0.5)     # top right
pic.draw()
win.flip()
core.wait(0.5)

pic.pos = (0.5, -0.5)    # bottom right
pic.draw()
win.flip()
core.wait(0.5)

pic.pos = (-0.5, -0.5)   # bottom left
pic.draw()
win.flip()
core.wait(0.5)

win.close()
core.quit()
It works, but it is painful. Sixteen lines of hopping, of which twelve are copies with only the position changed. Reading it, the eye must check each block carefully to confirm that it really is the same as the others. Copied code is where bugs breed: change the wait from 0.5 to 1.0 and you must remember to change it in four places, and the one place you forget becomes an inconsistency you may never notice. The experiment we build this afternoon repeats its trial routine twelve times, once per stimulus. We are not going to write it twelve times.
Python’s answer to repetition of this kind is the function: a named block of code that you define once and run as often as you like. You have been using functions all day. print(), len(), and win.flip() are all functions that someone else wrote. This chapter is where you write your own.
crumbs: 5 · Functions: Write Once, Use Many Times

title: 5 · Functions: Write Once, Use Many Times
text:
Defining and calling
A function definition has four parts: the keyword def, a name you choose, parentheses, and a colon, followed by an indented body. The same colon-and-indentation shape as loops and if statements.
def greet():
    print("Welcome to the experiment!")
The name follows the same rules as variable names: no spaces, no special characters, and ideally a word that says what the function does. Running a definition has a perhaps surprising property: it produces no output at all. Python reads the body, stores it under the name greet, and moves on. The body runs only when the function is called, which means written by name with parentheses: greet().
The distinction between defining and calling is the heart of this chapter, so let us test it immediately.
greet()
greet()
Welcome to the experiment!
Welcome to the experiment!

Three lines appear in the console after the following code. Give them in order, each on a new line.
def greet():
    print("Welcome!")

print("Experiment starting")
greet()
greet()

Python reads top to bottom. The definition stores the recipe without running it; the body runs only at each call. What executes first?


Experiment starting
Welcome!
Welcome!
The definition at the top produces no output; it only stores the body under the name greet. Execution begins with the first ordinary line, and the stored body runs once per call. One definition, two calls, two greetings.
crumbs: 5 · Functions: Write Once, Use Many Times

title: 5 · Functions: Write Once, Use Many Times
text:
Parameters: functions with input
A function that always does exactly the same thing has limited use. Functions become powerful when they accept parameters: variables that receive a value at each call. A parameter is named inside the parentheses of the definition. Each call then supplies a value, and inside the body the parameter behaves like an ordinary variable holding that value.
def greet(name):
    print(f"Welcome, {name}!")

greet("Anna")
greet("Chris")
Welcome, Anna!
Welcome, Chris!
Same function, different input, different behaviour. Inside the body, name is an ordinary variable, and the f-string inserts its value into the greeting. Notice the division of labour: the definition describes what happens in general, with the parameter standing in for whatever will vary; each call fills in the specifics.
This is exactly the structure of our rabbit hopping problem. The four blocks were identical in every respect except one value: the position. General behaviour, one varying value. That is a function with one parameter.
crumbs: 5 · Functions: Write Once, Use Many Times

title: 5 · Functions: Write Once, Use Many Times
text:
Rebuilding the hop
The repeated four lines become the body; the position becomes the parameter:
def show_rabbit(position):
    pic.pos = position
    pic.draw()
    win.flip()
    core.wait(0.5)
And the full script becomes:
from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1280, 720), fullscr=False,
                    color='black', checkTiming=False)

pic = visual.ImageStim(win, image='rabbit.jpg', size=0.5)

def show_rabbit(position):
    pic.pos = position
    pic.draw()
    win.flip()
    core.wait(0.5)

show_rabbit((-0.5, 0.5))    # top left
show_rabbit((0.5, 0.5))     # top right
show_rabbit((0.5, -0.5))    # bottom right
show_rabbit((-0.5, -0.5))   # bottom left

win.close()
core.quit()
Compare the two versions. The hopping section has shrunk from sixteen lines to four, and those four now read like a description of what happens rather than instructions for how. The cycle itself, move, draw, flip, wait, is written exactly once, inside the definition. To change the hop duration, you now edit one line, and every hop obeys. To add a fifth hop, you add one call.
Type this version into a new script, run it, and confirm the rabbit still visits all four corners.
crumbs: 5 · Functions: Write Once, Use Many Times

title: 5 · Functions: Write Once, Use Many Times
text:
A second function: showing text
Every experiment shows text screens: a welcome, instructions, a goodbye. The pattern is always the same four beats, so it deserves a function of its own. This one takes the text as its parameter and waits for a key press, so the participant reads at their own pace:
def msg(text):
    message = visual.TextStim(win, text=text, height=0.08)
    message.draw()
    win.flip()
    event.waitKeys()
One call now produces a complete, participant-paced text screen:
msg("Welcome to the experiment! Press any key to begin.")






Good to know: where functions go in a script



Definitions must run before the first call, because Python reads top to bottom: a call above its definition fails with a NameError. The convention for structure is:

imports at the top,
the window and stimuli
all function definitions together
the experiment itself at the bottom.

By following conventions, a reader can then find everything where they expect it.








Summary



Repetition invites bugs, and functions remove repetition. A function is defined once, with def, a name, parentheses, and an indented body, and it runs each time it is called by name with parentheses. A definition alone produces nothing; only the call executes. Parameters let one definition serve many cases: the part that varies becomes the input. The hop shrank from sixteen lines to one definition and four calls, and msg() does the same for text screens. Definitions go before calls, and a function that seems ignored is usually missing its parentheses.








Checkpoint · the refactored hop





from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1280, 720), fullscr=False,
                    color='black', checkTiming=False)

pic = visual.ImageStim(win, image='rabbit.jpg', size=0.5)

def show_rabbit(position):
    pic.pos = position
    pic.draw()
    win.flip()
    core.wait(0.5)

def msg(text):
    message = visual.TextStim(win, text=text, height=0.08)
    message.draw()
    win.flip()
    event.waitKeys()

msg("Watch the rabbit! Press any key to start.")

show_rabbit((-0.5, 0.5))
show_rabbit((0.5, 0.5))
show_rabbit((0.5, -0.5))
show_rabbit((-0.5, -0.5))

msg("Done! Press any key to close.")

win.close()
core.quit()



Rabbit hopping on function calls? Next: Reading in multiple files.

title: 3 · The Draw-Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)
text:
Two buffers: backstage and stage
Here is the single most important mechanic of the day. PsychoPy uses double buffering: there are two screen buffers, and you never draw directly onto the visible one. Showing a stimulus always takes three steps:

Prepare: create the stimulus object: stim = visual.TextStim(win, text='Hi!'). Nothing appears.
Draw: paint it onto the hidden back buffer: stim.draw(). Still nothing on screen!
Flip: swap the buffers: win.flip(). The prepared image appears, all at once.

Think of a theatre: the back buffer is backstage, the front buffer is the stage. You can arrange the whole scene backstage: draw as many stimuli as you like, and flip() raises the curtain in a single instant.
crumbs: Block 1 · From Python to a window
3 · The Draw-Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)

title: 3 · The Draw-Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)
text:
Why this design?
A typical monitor redraws 60 times per second, so one frame lasts ~16.7 ms. Because the swap happens between two refreshes, stimulus onset is a single, well-defined moment: the moment of the flip. In Block 3, we will reset a clock at exactly that moment to measure reaction times.
crumbs: Block 1 · From Python to a window
3 · The Draw-Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)

title: 3 · The Draw-Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)
text:
Hello, world: the full cycle
Type and run:
from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1080, 720), color='black',
                    fullscr=False, checkTiming=False)

text = visual.TextStim(win, text='Hello, world!',
                       color='white', height=0.1)
text.draw()      # paint it backstage
win.flip()       # curtain up!

event.waitKeys() # pause until any key is pressed

win.close()      # close the window
core.quit()      # end the session cleanly
You should see Hello, world! in white on black, staying until you press a key. The line doing the staying is event.waitKeys(): it pauses the script until any key is pressed. Which key, and what to do with that information, becomes important later on.

title: 3 · The Draw-Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)
text:
The sabotage lab
Now let’s break it on purpose to figure out what’s going on in the code: three times. Each sabotage teaches you to recognise one of today’s three most common bugs before it happens to you by accident. Think first, then actually run the broken script and watch.






🤔 Sabotage 1: think first



Delete the line win.flip(). What will you see when you run it?






Check your thinking





A blank black window. The text was drawn, but only to the back buffer, which was never swapped to the screen. Everything happened backstage; the curtain never rose. Blank screen almost always means a missing flip.











🤔 Sabotage 2: think first



Put win.flip() back. Now delete event.waitKeys(). What happens?






Check your thinking





The text flashes for a split second and vanishes. The script runs straight on to win.close(), and closing the window takes the text with it. Every flip needs a waiting step after it: a keypress wait like before, or a timed core.wait() as in the next chapter. If this is missing, the participant sees almost nothing.











🤔 Sabotage 3: think first



Restore everything. Now delete the last two lines (win.close() and core.quit()). What happens after you press a key?






Check your thinking





Quite possibly… nothing different! On modern PsychoPy the window usually closes anyway when the script ends. So why do we insist on those two lines? Because usually is not a word you want in an experiment: on some machines and older versions, the window lingers as a frozen zombie, and in longer scripts an un-closed window can hold resources or hide error messages. win.close() and core.quit() make the shutdown explicit and guaranteed instead of a lucky side effect.





Repair your script so all three sabotages are undone, and run it once more to prove it.

title: 3 · The Draw-Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)
text:
Your first debugging
You’ve now caused all three diseases, so you can diagnose them. This is the skill that saves you time all afternoon:

Your neighbour’s script runs without errors, but their window is plain black: no text, nothing. Which line have they most likely forgotten?

If draw() were missing you’d also see nothing, but the far more common culprit is the step after drawing. What raises the curtain?


win.flip(): the stimulus was prepared and probably drawn, but never swapped to the visible screen. Blank-but-running is the flip’s signature symptom. (A missing draw() produces the same blankness and is the second guess, but forgetting the flip will be today’s most common bug by a wide margin.)


Say the mantra once: prepare, draw, flip, wait. You now have the day’s core mechanic memorised.

title: 3 · The Draw-Flip Cycle (and How to Break It)
text:
Load up a visual stimulus
Time for your first image, and the good news is that you already know how this works. An image follows the same cycle as text; the only change is the type of stimulus you prepare. Where text uses TextStim with a text argument, images use ImageStim with an image argument naming a file:
img = visual.ImageStim(win, image='rabbit.jpg')
img.draw()
win.flip()
Prepare, draw, flip: nothing else is new. What you need is the file itself. Download the rabbit and save it in the same folder as your script:
⬇️ Download rabbit.jpg
Now modify your Chapter 3 script: after the Hello, world! screen, show the rabbit, participant-paced. Run it.






Show the code





from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(size=(1280, 720), color='black',
                    fullscr=False, checkTiming=False)

img = visual.ImageStim(win, image='rabbit.jpg')
img.draw()
win.flip()
event.waitKeys()

win.close()
core.quit()









Where Python looks for images



'rabbit.jpg' is a relative path: Python looks for the file in the same folder as your script. If the image refuses to load, the file and the script are not sitting together. That is the most common little stumble of the day, and the fix is just moving a file.








Summary



Showing a stimulus is always three steps: prepare the object, draw it to the hidden back buffer, flip the buffers to reveal it, then wait, or the participant sees nothing. The flip is a single, precisely-timed moment, which is what makes reaction-time measurement possible. And the three sabotages gave you the diagnostic table: blank screen → likely a missing flip; content flashing past → missing wait; lingering window → missing cleanup. Prepare, draw, flip, wait.

subject_id = "S_07"

:.2f rounds to two decimals. Which way does 0.5391 go?

filename = "gear_R.jpg"
parts = filename.split("_")
print(parts[1])

What prints?

Nearly! There’s only one underscore, so only one cut. What stays attached to the R?


parts[1]: which piece is at index 1? Count from zero.

4: Loops & conditionals
words = ['tea', 'coffee', 'water', 'juice']
words.append('cocoa')

for w in words:
    if len(w) > 5:
        print(w.upper())
    else:
        print(w)

What does this print? One line, in order, separated by spaces.

Careful: how many letters does cocoa have, exactly? And is 5 > 5 true?


Which words have more than 5 letters? Count before you uppercase.


Five lines: tea, COFFEE, water, juice, cocoa. Only coffee exceeds five letters. The word cocoa has exactly five, and 5 > 5 is False. This combination of a loop and a conditional is the skeleton of the trial loop you will build today.

section: 5: Nested loops: looping inside the items
text:
5: Nested loops: looping inside the items
Here we have a loop inside a loop, as in Session 1’s Exercise 3. Recall that a string is itself iterable: its elements are its characters:
keys = ['left', 'up']

for key in keys:
    print(key)
    for character in key:
        print(character)

How many lines does this print in total?

Count both levels: each key is printed once in full, and then once per character. How many characters in left? In up?


The outer loop prints each key once in full. The inner loop then iterates over that key’s characters, printing one line per character.


8 lines: for each key: the whole word once, then its characters one by one:
left
l
e
f
t
up
u
p
Each time, it first prints the whole word. Then the inner loop goes through that word one character at a time, printing each one. So left gives 1 line for the word plus 4 lines for its letters, and up gives 1 plus 2. Notice that Python decides what the loop variable holds by looking at what comes after in: a list gives you its items, a string gives you its characters. The names key and character are just labels we chose; they do not tell Python anything.

text:
6 · Testing how a string ends
.endswith() returns True or False, so it can serve directly as the condition of an if statement. Our stimulus filenames use this: the suffix _L or _R records which response is correct.
stimuli = ['wheel_L.jpg', 'wheel_R.jpg', 'gear_L.jpg']

for s in stimuli:
    if s.endswith("_L.jpg"):
        print(s, '-> left')
    else:
        print(s, '-> right')

Which direction is assigned to each filename? Answer in order, on one line.

Test each filename’s ending against "_L.jpg". Which of the three match?


left, right, left. The two filenames ending in _L.jpg pass the test; wheel_R.jpg fails it and falls to the else branch. Remember this construction: in the feedback chapter it determines which key the participant should have pressed.

title: 1 · Warming Up: A Python Refresher
text:
7: The finale: everything at once
stimuli = ['wheel_L.jpg', 'wheel_R.jpg', 'gear_L.jpg']
trial = 0

for s in stimuli:
    trial += 1
    if s.endswith("_L.jpg"):
        answer = "left"
    else:
        answer = "right"
    print(f"Trial {trial}: {s}, {answer} is the correct answer")

Write out the full output, one line per trial, exactly as it will appear in the console.

The counter starts at 0, but trial += 1 runs before the print. What is its value on the first trial?


Very close. Compare your punctuation with the f-string: is there a full stop at the end?


Trial 1: wheel_L.jpg, left is the correct answer
Trial 2: wheel_R.jpg, right is the correct answer
Trial 3: gear_L.jpg, left is the correct answer
Consider what you have just written from memory: a stimulus list, a trial counter, a filename check that determines the correct answer, and an f-string that reports each trial. This is the complete logical skeleton of today’s experiment. The only missing element is a screen, which the next chapter provides.

title: 6 · Functions & modules
text:
What is a function?
A function is like a recipe: it contains instructions that run when you call it by name.
Let’s say we want to make a Python function that prints “This is a greeting” every time it runs. We will call the function greeting. First, the definition syntax:
def function_name():
     # instructions go here
Let’s now try defining the function greeting:
# Define the function.
def greeting():
     print("This is a greeting")
Once Python has evaluated the definition, the function can be called by name and its contents will execute.
greeting()
This calls the function and the output should be:
This is a greeting
Note that running the definition printed nothing. The body only runs when the function is called.

title: 6 · Functions & modules
section: Everything that happens inside a function stays inside a function (unless otherwise specified)
text:
Everything that happens inside a function stays inside a function (unless otherwise specified)
Let’s define variables inside the function greeting:
def greeting():
    casual = "hey"
    formal = "hello"

    print(casual)
    print(formal)
And now call the function:
greeting()
hey
hello

Now type casual into the console and press Enter. What happens?

Would Python know what casual is out here? Where was it created?


A NameError: Python does not know casual out here, because it was created inside the function. By default, variables created inside functions have local scope: they can only be accessed from inside that function.

title: 6 · Functions & modules
text:
Function outputs and inputs
Although local variables cannot normally be accessed outside a function, the return statement sends values back to the code that called the function. Let’s return both casual and formal from greeting:
def greeting():
    casual = "hey"
    formal = "hello"

    print(casual)
    print(formal)

    return casual, formal
Now we can call the function and store its returned values in variables:
# Store the returned values in two separate variables.
casual_greeting, formal_greeting = greeting()

# Store both returned values in one tuple.
greeting_types = greeting()
In the first case, the two returned values are unpacked into two separate variables. In the second case, both values are stored in a tuple. A tuple is like a list, but its values cannot be changed. It is indexed the same way as a list: greeting_types[0] and greeting_types[1].
We can also pass inputs to functions. Imagine that we want greeting to print either a casual or a formal greeting depending on our relationship with the person being greeted. We can pass that information as an input.
def greeting(relation_to_greeted_person):
    casual = "hey"
    formal = "hello"

    if relation_to_greeted_person == "friend":
        print(casual)
        return casual
    else:
        print(formal)
        return formal
Now call the function with an input value. Inside the function, that value is stored in relation_to_greeted_person:
greeting_type = greeting("friend")
print(greeting_type)
>>> hey  # printed inside the function
>>> hey  # printed by print(greeting_type)
Two heys: one printed inside the function, one by our print(greeting_type). The function both printed and returned.
We can pass multiple input arguments too:
def greeting(relation_to_greeted_person, name):
    casual = "hey"
    formal = "hello"

    if relation_to_greeted_person == "friend":
        print(f"{casual} {name}!")
        return casual
    else:
        print(f"{formal} {name}!")
        return formal
greeting_type = greeting("friend", "anna")
hey anna!

The call printed hey anna!. But what value is now stored in greeting_type? (Check the return line before answering.)

hey anna! is what got printed, but look at what the function returns. Are they the same thing?


hey: the function returns casual, not the personalised f-string it printed. What a function shows and what it hands back are independent, and only the returned value lands in the variable. (And note: assigning a return value does not display it. To see it, print(greeting_type) explicitly.)

title: 6 · Functions & modules
text:
Modules
Functions can become lengthy, and it can be inconvenient to define every function in the main code file for a project. To keep your code organized, you can store function definitions in a separate Python file: a .py file containing reusable code is called a module, and it works like a small library of functions.
To use a function from a module, import the module where you are working:
# In greeting_types.py:
def greetings():
    print("Hello, world!")
After creating greeting_types.py and defining greetings() there, import the module in the console or another Python file:
import greeting_types

greeting_types.greetings()
Hello, world!
The pattern is module name, dot, function: greeting_types.greetings().






Summary



Functions are reusable recipes that can accept inputs and return outputs, and what they print is not what they return. Variables inside them are local. Modules are Python files that help organize and reuse functions, unlocked with import.


Lesson learned? Next: Exercise 4: Putting it all together — Logical operations & functions.

Remember that we need to reinstall packages in UCloud every time we start a new job, because each job is assigned to a new remote computer. The same is true for Python: we need to install the Python language extension in the Coder application each time we start a new job. Here’s how:

title: 1 · Getting Started: Setting up your Python environment
section: Create your first Python code file
text:
Create your first Python code file
You can now create a new Python code file. Here’s how:

In the far-left panel, find the icon that looks like three horizontal lines stacked on top of each other. Click it.

“Hello world!”: Run your first line of Python code
In your new code file, enter your first line of Python code:
print("Hello world!")

Your first prediction! Throughout these sessions, boxes like this ask you to guess what code will do before you run it. That’s where the learning happens, and wrong guesses are very welcome and encouraged. After a few tries the box will offer to show you the answer, so you can never get stuck. So: what exactly will appear in the console when this line runs? Take a guess.

Hello world!. Note that there are no quotation marks. The quotes tell Python where the text starts and ends; they are not part of the text itself.


Now run the code by highlighting it and pressing Shift+Enter. You should see a dedicated terminal open below.
Terminal shows what you expected? Next: Chapter 2 — Variables and types.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text: Welcome! Over the coming workshop sessions, you’ll go from typing your very first line of Python to watching a full behavioural experiment run on your own screen: window, stimuli, responses, feedback, the lot. Between you and that moment stand a handful of Python concepts and a few dozen extremely fixable error messages. We assume no programming experience. If you can rename a file, you’re qualified to start.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
Why programming?
Nearly every empirical experiment in cognitive science (e.g. reaction-time studies, reading paradigms, eye-tracking, EEG) is implemented in code. A working knowledge of Python allows you to build precisely the experiment your research question requires, to understand the structure and provenance of your data, and to diagnose problems when they arise.
The aim of these three sessions is a modest form of fluency: by the end, the experiment running on your screen should be a system you can read, modify, and reason about. These skills will hopefully outlast the course: designing, implementing, and troubleshooting your own experiments is part of the everyday craft of working scientists, in cognitive science and well beyond.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
Why Python and not R?
The Python programming language is optimal for coding experiments because it has a special library called PsychoPy for doing so.
In contrast, the R programming language is optimal for statistical analyses, as it was designed specifically for this purpose.
Therefore, this workshop on programming for experiments focuses on Python instead of R, which you instead cover in your Methods 1 practical classes.
However, as you will learn over the course of the semester, many of the programming concepts that we cover in Session 1 are generalizable to R and all other languages.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
The three sessions
Session 1 · Python basics Variables, lists, loops, conditionals, functions. These are the handful of building blocks that all programs are made of. Everything you learn here gets used directly in Session 2.
[Session 2 · Introduction to PsychoPy] (materials coming) PsychoPy is the Python library psychologists use to run experiments: it opens windows, draws stimuli, and records keypresses with precise timing. You build an experiment step by step and leave with a script that runs: images in random order, keyboard responses, feedback on every trial, and more..
Session 3 · From cogwheels to words (materials coming) Swap the images for words, add a clock and a logfile, and your CogWheel script becomes a self-paced reading experiment, the direct starting point for your Portfolio 2 prototype.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
How the sessions work
Each session follows the same rhythm: a short lecture introduces the concepts and demonstrates them live, and you then put them to work in a set of exercises you complete on your own, at your own pace, with the teaching team circulating. Three habits will serve you well throughout:

Predict before you run. Whenever you see a 🔮 Predict first box, write down what the code will do before running it.
Run constantly. Run your code after every small change, not after twenty lines. Small steps make bugs easy to find.
Never stay stuck. Ten minutes on the same bug is the signal to ask: check the error message, unfold the solution, or wave a teacher over. Sitting silently with a bug is the one wrong way to use these sessions.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
What you need

Your own laptop with PsychoPy installed. Install instructions are sent out before Session 2, and each session starts with a setup check. If the install fights back, come 15 minutes early.
Curiosity. A willingness to try things, break things, and read the occasional error message will carry you further than any prior experience would.

Ready? Start with Session 1.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text: Block 2 · Chapter 2 of 3 before the first break. Understand what a variable is in Python & the different types of variables.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
What is a variable?
A variable is a name we give to a value so we can store it and use it later in our code. The name stays the same, but the value stored in it can change while the program is running. A variable can store a number, a word, or a list of values.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Your first variable
Let’s create our first variable in Python. We will call it my_name and store a name in it.
my_name = "anna"
We can also add comments to explain what our code is doing. In Python, a comment starts with #. Everything after # on that line is ignored by Python.
# This variable stores my name.
my_name = "anna"
Now run the code by selecting it in your file and pressing Shift+Enter.
You will see the code executed in the console below. If you then type my_name on a new line and press Enter, Python will print the value stored in the variable:
>>> my_name = 'anna'
>>> my_name
'anna'
An easier way to see the output is to use the print() function:
# This variable stores my name.
my_name = "anna"

# This line prints the value stored in my_name.
print(my_name)
Select these lines and press Shift+Enter. You should see the value of my_name appear in the console.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Variable types
Python allows us to create variables that store different kinds of data. Today we will focus on some of the most common variable types.
We can find the type of a variable by using the type() function:
# Query the type of my_name.
type(my_name)
This returns <class 'str'>, which means that my_name is a string variable.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Data Type 1: Regular string variables
String variables are defined by strings of characters. String variables are specified using single or double quotation marks around the string.
# If you use single quotes here, it won't work. Why?
dog_name_possessive = 'anna's dog's name is..'

# If you use double-quotes here it will work. 
dog_name_possessive = "anna's dog's name is.."






🤔 Think first



Why does the single-quoted version fail while the double-quoted version works?






Check your thinking





The apostrophe in anna’s ends the single-quoted string early. Python thinks the string stops after anna, and the rest is nonsense to it. Double quotes let Python see the apostrophe as just another character inside the string.






Indexing
Strings are stored like arrays of characters, meaning that you can individually access single characters in the string using indexing (square brackets around the indices you want to extract).
# Here you are indexing the first 4 characters in the variable my_name_possessive. 
# You use square brackets around the indices that you want to extract.
dog_name_possessive[0:4] # extract 4 characters from the 0th character.

# you can also count backwards from the end of a string using the minus sign, e.g.:
dog_name_possessive[-4:]
You may have noticed that we start indexing at 0 instead of 1. This is because Python is a zero-indexed language, so whenever you have a multi-item variable, the first item is always indexed using 0 instead of 1. CAREFUL: R is a 1-indexed langauge, so you always index the first item in a multi-item variable using 1 in R instead of 0.

Before you run it: what will dog_name_possessive[0:4] give you?

anna: characters 0, 1, 2 and 3. The index range [0:4] starts at 0 and stops before 4, so you get exactly 4 characters. (The console shows it wrapped in quotes ('anna') because it is a string.)

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
String methods
String variables have many built-in methods that we can call on them. Here are some useful string methods:

split()
If you type the name of your string variable followed by .split(), Python splits the string into smaller pieces, using the space character as the default delimiter. Try it in the console:
dog_name_possessive.split()
>>> ["anna's", "dog's", 'name', 'is..']
The split() method returns a list of strings. Each item is one part of the original text, separated by the chosen delimiter.
You can store the output in a variable, and since it is a list, you can index it, even down to characters within each item:
split_variable = dog_name_possessive.split()
split_variable[0]
split_variable[0][0]  # first letter of first word.
split_variable[1][1]  # second letter of second word.
>>> split_variable[0]
>>> "anna's"
>>> split_variable[0][0]  # first letter of first word.
>>> 'a'
>>> split_variable[1][1]  # second letter of second word.
>>> 'o'
So split_variable[1][1] means: take item 1 of the list ("dog's": remember, zero-indexed!), then character 1 of that string.
You can also use split() with a different delimiter, such as an underscore:
subject_id = "S_01"
subject_id.split("_")
>>> ['S', '01']

Given responses = "left right left left", what does responses.split() return?

['left', 'right', 'left', 'left']: a list of four strings, one per word. Repeats are kept; split() just cuts, it doesn’t deduplicate.



Given date = "2026-09-14", what does date.split("-") return?

The delimiter is the cut line. It doesn’t survive into the pieces.


['2026', '09', '14']. Three pieces, dashes gone. Note they are strings, not numbers: '09' keeps its leading zero, and you couldn’t do maths with it without converting first.




upper()
The upper() method converts all letters in a string to uppercase.
name = "anna"
name.upper()
>>> 'ANNA'
Note that upper() does not change name itself — it returns a new, uppercased string. If you want to keep it, store it:
name_upper = name.upper()
print(name_upper)
>>> ANNA
# or store the result in a new variable.
name_upper = name.upper()
print(name_upper)
Here are a few more useful string methods:
word = " subject_01 "
print(word.lower())
print(word.strip())
print(word.replace("p", "P"))
print(word.startswith(" "))
print(word.endswith(" "))


len()
And, finally, we can get the length of a string variable using len() (not a string-specific method)
len(word)
>>> 12
The 10 characters of subject_01 plus the two spaces. Invisible characters count, which is exactly why .strip() exists.
There’s lots more that you can do with strings, but these are the basics!

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Data Type 2: Regular numeric variables
Now let’s turn to our other fundamental variable type: numeric. There are two basic numeric types:

Integers: whole numbers (no decimal point)
Floating points: numbers with a decimal point

# This is an integer.
a = 1
type(a)
>>> int
# This is a floating point.
b = 1.5
type(b)
>>> float
c = 1.00

c stores the value one, but what does type(c) return? float or int?

<class 'float'>: a floating point. The value is a whole number, but writing it with a decimal point makes it a float. What matters is how it is written, not what it equals.


The same logic applies to operations:
# What happens when you combine types in operations?
d = b + c
type(d)
>>> float
Adding the float b to the float c gives a float — d is 2.5. And even when an operation on two floats produces a whole number, the result stays a floating point:
e = 1.5 + 1.5
type(e)
print(e)
<class 'float'>
3.0
The value is three — but Python shows it as 3.0: the .0 is the float’s badge. It never silently becomes an integer.
Standard numeric operations are addition (shown above), subtraction, multiplication and division:
print(a - b)   # subtraction
print(a * b)   # multiplication
print(a / b)   # division
-0.5
1.5
0.6666666666666666

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Printing variables with f-strings
Imagine that you want to print reaction times for a given subject on an experiment screen. The subject is different in each experiment, and so is their reaction time.
You can create a special expression called an f-string, where you embed variables inside a string: start the string with f, then place variable names inside curly brackets {}.
subject_id = "S_01"
reaction_time = 0.45
message = f"Reaction time for {subject_id}: {reaction_time:.2f} seconds"
Here {subject_id} inserts the value of the subject ID variable, and {reaction_time:.2f} inserts the value of reaction_time, where .2f formats the number with two digits after the decimal point.

What exactly does print(message) show?

Reaction time for S_01: 0.45 seconds: the curly-bracket parts are replaced by the variables’ values, and everything else is printed as-is. In Session 2, messages like this become the text you show on the experiment screen.


All predictions checked? Next: Exercise 1 — Variables & data types.

title: 3 · Lists
text: Block 3 · Chapter 4 of the day. Understand what a list is and how to use lists effectively.

title: 3 · Lists
text:
What are lists?
A list is, literally, a list of items, stored in order, that can be changed (lists are mutable, a word that will matter shortly). You define one with square brackets, items separated by commas:
variable_name = [item1, item2, item3]
Lists can contain items of the same type or of different types, and this is the data structure experiments run on: a list of stimuli, a list of responses, a list of reaction times.

title: 3 · Lists
text:
Making lists
You can create lists with all strings, all numeric data, or a combination:
# First, simple lists of same-type items.
shopping = ["apples", "pears", "bananas"]
test_scores = [90, 60, 100, 82]

# Now mixed items.
mixed_list = ["cats", 7, 309.45]

print(test_scores)
print(mixed_list)
>>> [90, 60, 100, 82]
>>> ['cats', 7, 309.45]
You can also put lists inside lists:
combined = [shopping, test_scores, mixed_list]
print(combined)
>>> [['apples', 'pears', 'bananas'], [90, 60, 100, 82], ['cats', 7, 309.45]]
Three items: each of which is itself a list. Keep that picture in mind for the prediction below.

title: 3 · Lists
text:
Indexing lists
We index lists just like we indexed character strings: square brackets after the name, index inside.
print(shopping[0])
print(shopping[1])
print(shopping[2])
apples
pears
bananas
You may recognise this syntax from the previous block. That’s because we were already working with lists when we used .split(): splitting a string returns a list, and everything you learned there (zero-indexing, negative indexing, two brackets for two levels) applies to all lists.

Sub-indexing, then: what does shopping[0][0:2] return?

That’s shopping[0]: the whole first item. The second bracket slices into that string: which characters does [0:2] take?


'ap': shopping[0] picks the string 'apples' out of the list, and [0:2] slices characters 0 and 1 out of that string. Stops before 2, as always.



And the list of lists: what does combined[1] give you?

Close if you answered 60, but count the brackets. One pair of brackets goes one level deep. What lives at position 1 of combined?


[90, 60, 100, 82] — the entire second list. combined’s items are whole lists, so one index retrieves a whole list. To reach 60 you’d go two levels: combined[1][1].

title: 3 · Lists
text:
Changing list items
Lists are mutable: we can change their contents after creating them. Remember upper(), which returned a new string and left the original untouched? Lists are the opposite. These operations change the list itself, in place. Three ways to do it:

Replace an item, using indexing.
Append an item to the end.
Insert an item at a chosen position.

Predict each print() before you run it. This is where the bracket-counting pays off. Our starting point:
print(shopping)
['apples', 'pears', 'bananas']
Replace the second item:
shopping[1] = "kiwi"
print(shopping)
['apples', 'kiwi', 'bananas']
Goodbye pears: index 1 is the second item. Now append:
shopping.append("raspberry")
print(shopping)
['apples', 'kiwi', 'bananas', 'raspberry']
append() always adds at the end. Finally, insert at a particular position:
shopping.insert(1, "blueberry")

The finale: what does print(shopping) show now? Type the full list.

Almost — insert(1, ...) puts the new item at index 1, and everything from there shifts right. Who ends up second?


['apples', 'blueberry', 'kiwi', 'bananas', 'raspberry']. insert(1, ...) places blueberry at index 1 and shifts kiwi, bananas and raspberry one step right. Nothing is overwritten. That’s the difference from shopping[1] = ..., which replaces.


In the PsychoPy sessions, these operations will become very familiar: stimuli is a list of image filenames, responses.append(key) collects what the participant pressed, and shuffling a list gives every participant their own trial order.
All predictions checked? Next: Exercise 2 — Lists.

title: 4 · Loops
text: Block 3 · Chapter follows Exercise 2. Understand basic for and while loops.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
What is a loop?
A loop is a programming structure that repeats a block of code. In this lesson you will meet the two common types:

For loops repeat code once for each item in a collection, such as a list.
While loops repeat code while a condition is true.

This is the single most important chapter of the day for what comes next: when we start learning PsychoPy, we’ll learn that an experiment is a loop: for each stimulus: show it, record a response, give feedback.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
For loops
Imagine you have five subject IDs and want to print each one. You could write a separate print() for every subject:
print("S01")
print("S02")
...
print("S05")
This becomes repetitive and difficult to update. Instead, store the IDs in a list and loop through the items:
subject_ids = ['S01', 'S02', 'S03', 'S04', 'S05']

for subject in subject_ids:
    print(subject)
>>> S01
>>> S02
>>> S03
>>> S04
>>> S05
In plain language: for every item in subject_ids, store that item in subject and print it. Notice the syntax: the for statement ends with a colon, and the next line is indented. That indented part is the body of the loop, and it runs once per item. Each repetition is called an iteration; during each one, subject temporarily holds the current ID.

Your turn. Using a list from Exercise 2: what does this print?
animals = ['cat', 'dog', 'owl']
for animal in animals:
    print(animal)

The loop variable holds one item at a time. Not the list, and not the word “animals”.


Three lines: cat, dog, owl; one iteration per item, one print per iteration.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
Looping by index
You can also loop through the index positions of a list. This is useful when you need both an item’s position and its value:
# Get the total number of subjects.
number_of_subjects = len(subject_ids)

# Create indices from 0 up to, but not including, number_of_subjects.
subject_index_range = range(number_of_subjects)

# Use each index to retrieve the corresponding subject ID.
for index in subject_index_range:
    print(f"Subject {index + 1}: {subject_ids[index]}")
Subject 1: S01
Subject 2: S02
Subject 3: S03
Subject 4: S04
Subject 5: S05
Look closely at index + 1: the indices run 0-4 (zero-indexed, as ever), but humans count subjects from 1, so we print index + 1 while using plain index for the lookup.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
Counter variables
Sometimes you need to update a number on every iteration. This number is called a counter variable — here counting how many days have been processed:
weekdays = ['monday', 'tuesday', 'wednesday', 'thursday', 'friday', 'saturday', 'sunday']

# Start a counter at zero.
day_of_week = 0

# Print each day, then add 1 to the counter.
for day in weekdays:
    print(f"The current day is {day}")
    day_of_week += 1
The current day is monday
The current day is tuesday
The current day is wednesday
The current day is thursday
The current day is friday
The current day is saturday
The current day is sunday
(+= 1 is shorthand for day_of_week = day_of_week + 1. Add one to what’s there.). Notice the syntax: the for statement ends with a colon, and the loop body must be indented.

After the loop finishes, we print the counter:
print(f"There are {day_of_week} days in the list.")
What exactly appears?

Careful. The counter started at 0, but it was incremented once for every item. How many increments happened?


There are 7 days in the list.. The counter went 0→7, one += 1 per iteration. Starting at 0 doesn’t mean ending one short: seven items, seven increments.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
While loops
While loops repeat a block of code while a condition is True. You will learn more about conditions in the logical-operations lesson. For now, read this example and predict before running:
day_of_week = 0

while day_of_week < 6:
    print(f"The current day is {weekdays[day_of_week]}")
    # Move to the next index so the condition will eventually become False.
    day_of_week += 1

Before you run it: how many lines does this print?

The condition is day_of_week < 6: strictly less than. Which values of the counter pass that test?


6 lines: monday through saturday. The counter values 0,1,2,3,4,5 pass the < 6 test; when it reaches 6, the condition is False and the loop stops before printing sunday. < versus <= is a one-character difference with a one-iteration consequence.


One warning while we’re here: the comment in the body is not decoration. If you forget the day_of_week += 1, the condition never becomes False — and the loop runs forever. It happens to everyone once; when it happens to you, click the console and press Ctrl-C to stop it.






Summary



Loops repeat code. Use a for loop to work through each item in a collection, and an index-based for loop when you also need each item’s position. A counter variable records progress by changing on every iteration. Use a while loop when repetition should continue only while a condition is True, and make sure something in the body eventually makes it False.


Predictions checked? Next: Exercise 3: Loops.

title: 5 · Logical operations
text: Block 4 · Understand relational and logical operators: the decision-making machinery behind every experiment.

title: 5 · Logical operations
text:
What is a relational operator?
We often want to write code that makes relational comparisons. A relational comparison assesses the relationship between two different values, such as whether one value is greater than, less than, or equal to another. Python has several built-in relational operators:
1 < 2    # Less than
1 > 2    # Greater than
1 <= 2   # Less than or equal to
1 >= 2   # Greater than or equal to
1 == 2   # Equal to
1 != 2   # Not equal to
True
False
True
False
False
True
Note the double equals: == compares, while a single = assigns. Mixing them up is one of the most common bugs in beginner code (Python will refuse to run if x = 1:, which is its way of protecting you).






🤔 Think first



Why do these relational comparisons return only True or False, never a number or a string?






Check your thinking





A relational comparison checks a single condition, and a condition can only hold or not hold: 1 < 2 is either true or it isn’t. There is no third option. This yes/no output is called a Boolean value, and it is exactly what if statements (below) run on.

title: 5 · Logical operations
text:
What is a logical operator?
Relational operators compare two values. Logical operators combine the results of multiple comparisons:
True and True    # and: True only when both sides are True.
True or False    # or: True when at least one side is True.
True != False    # xor: True when exactly one side is True.
>>> True
>>> True
>>> True
Now let’s put this into context. Predict all four before running:
x = 1
y = 2
z = 3

y > x and z > x           # both sides true?
y < x or z < x            # at least one side true?
(x == y) != (y > x)       # exactly one side true?
y > x and z > x and 10 > x  # operators can chain: every side must be true.

What do the four expressions return, in order?

Check the or line again — but also the xor: (x == y) is False and (y > x) is True. Are those results different from each other?


True, False, True, True.
The or line is False: it needs at least one true side, but y < x and z < x are both false. The xor line is True: False != True — the two conditions disagree, which is exactly what xor detects.








🤔 Think first



Why are there parentheses around the comparisons in the xor line, but not in the other logical operations?






Check your thinking





The parentheses make Python evaluate (x == y) and (y > x) first, then compare those two Boolean results with !=. Without them, Python reads x == y != y > x as one chained comparison — a different (and here, misleading) computation. When combining complete conditions, parentheses make your intention unambiguous — to Python and to the humans reading your code.

title: 5 · Logical operations
section: If statements: putting operators to work
text:
If statements: putting operators to work
Now, very excitingly, we can use operators inside if statements, which evaluate a condition and execute the code inside them only if the condition is met:
x = 1
y = 2
z = 3

# The indented code runs *only if* x < y evaluates to True.
if x < y:
    print(x < y)
>>> True
Here x is indeed less than y, so the condition holds and the code inside the statement runs. The syntax pattern (notice the colon and the indentation: same shape as loops):
if some_condition_that_is_true_or_false:
    code that runs ONLY when the condition is True
Because the indented code is executed only conditionally, if statements are called control flow statements: they control which code runs.

If–else statements
The final flourish for today. Suppose you want to run one line when a condition is true and a different line when it is not: enter if-else:
if x < y:
    print(f"{x} is less than {y}")
else:
    print(f"{x} is not less than {y}")  # runs *only* when the condition fails.
>>> 1 is less than 2
Note the colon after else and the indentation: the same syntax rules as if. We can of course use logical operators in the condition:
if x < y and x == 1:
    print(f"{x} is less than {y} and equals 1")
else:
    print(f"{x} is not both less than {y} and equal to 1")
>>> 1 is less than 2 and equals 1
Finally, conditions can have more than two branches. elif tests a new condition when the previous one failed, and statements can even be nested:
if x < 10:
    if x == 1:
        print("x is equal to 1")
    elif x == 2:
        print("x is equal to 2")
    else:
        print("x is less than 10 but not equal to 1 or 2")
else:
    print("x is 10 or more")

Suppose we set x = 2 and run the nested block. What prints?

True, 2 is less than 10, so we enter the outer block. But then the inner checks run: which one catches x = 2 first?


x is equal to 2: the outer if x < 10 passes, then the inner if x == 1 fails, so the elif x == 2 gets its turn and matches. Only one branch of an if/elif/else chain ever runs: the first one whose condition is True.



And a naming question: what does elif stand for in plain language?

Else if: test another condition, but only when the preceding if (or elif) came up False.








Summary



You have learned to perform basic Boolean operations. Operations that result in true-or-false output. Relational operators compare values; logical operators combine the Boolean results of two or more conditions. And if, if–else, elif and nested statements let those conditions control which code runs. In the PsychoPy sessions, this is precisely how feedback works: if the participant pressed the correct key, show the success image, else, show failure.


Predictions checked? Next: Functions.

text:
The PsychoPy application
Experiments need a screen: stimuli to look at, keys to press, precise timing. This is what PsychoPy adds. PsychoPy is free, open-source, and made by psychologists for psychologists (Peirce, 2007). PsychoPy uses ordinary Python, the Python you already know, plus a collection of ready-made tools for experiments.

title: 2 · Meet PsychoPy: Import, Modules, and a Window
text:
The import line
The Standalone PsychoPy app you installed contains everything: Python itself, plus all of PsychoPy’s tools. But installed only means the tools are on your computer, like books in a library building. Each script must still say which tools it wants on its desk. That is what an import does, and it is the first line of every experiment you will ever write:
from psychopy import visual, event, core
Read it aloud: from the PsychoPy collection, fetch three modules: visual, event, and core. A module is a bundle of related functions someone else wrote. Importing it makes its functions available in your script, called with a dot: visual.Window(...), core.wait(...) — module name, dot, function. (The dot should feel familiar: it’s the same dot as name.upper().)
If you forget the import line, Python greets you with NameError: name 'visual' is not defined. The tools exist on the computer, but your script never fetched them. You might see this error today; now you know what it means.
crumbs: Block 1 · From Python to a window

title: 2 · Meet PsychoPy: Import, Modules, and a Window
text:
Three modules, three different jobs

visual: everything the participant sees: the window, text, images.
event: everything the participant does: key presses.
core: time and control: waiting, clocks, quitting cleanly.


A quick mental map. Which module provides each step of the following sequence: show an image, wait for the participant’s keypress, then hold a blank screen for a moment before the next trial? Three names, in order, on one line.

Read the order asked: image, then keypress, then pause. Which module owns the keypress?


visual, event, core: sees, does, time. Notice what you just described: show a stimulus, collect a response, pause between trials. That is the trial structure you will build this afternoon. Every PsychoPy function you meet today lives in one of these three modules.


Opening PsychoPy for the first time can be confusing, because the app is really three programs in one:

Builder: a graphical interface for assembling experiments by dragging components. We do not use it. Everything we build, we write ourselves.
Coder: a text editor with a Run button. This is where we work all day. It is the counterpart of UCloud’s editor, but is a different program.
Runner: a small window that lists the scripts you have run and shows their output. It usually opens by itself alongside the others; you can mostly ignore it.

If PsychoPy opens in the Builder, switch to the Coder through the menu: View → Open Coder view. You can close the Builder window afterwards.

text:
Create your first window
Create a new script as just described and call it my_first_window.py. Type the following into it. Save it as my_first_window.py, and press the green Run button. (Note the environment change from UCloud: the Coder runs your whole script, top to bottom. No selecting lines, no Shift+Enter.)
from psychopy import visual, event, core

win = visual.Window(
    size=(500, 720),     # Width and height in pixels.
    color='grey',        # Background colour.
    fullscr=False,        # Keep False while developing.
    checkTiming=False)    # Skips a startup screen that measures your monitor. We do not need it.

core.wait(5)
win.close()
core.quit()
A grey window should appear for five seconds, then close. Not too exciting yet, but notice that win is a variable, like any from Session 1. It holds a window object, and that object has functions attached, called with a dot: win.close() now.






The escape hatch (you will need it today)



Sooner or later a window will freeze on you. It happens to everyone. Click on the Coder’s console and press Ctrl-C (or close the window via the taskbar). This is exactly why we develop with fullscr=False: a small window is much easier to escape.


Did the window open for five seconds and close by itself? Then you have imported modules and commanded a screen. Next: the Draw-Flip Cycle.
